title: A Co-Owner Wants to Sell Jointly Owned Property: What the Other Co-Owners Can Do
meta_description: Can a co-owner sell jointly owned property without consent? What Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act allows, and the remedies open to the rest.
intro: Yes, a co-owner can sell their own undivided share in jointly owned property without the consent of the other co-owners, and that sale is valid to the extent of that share. What the selling co-owner cannot do is sell the whole property as if it were theirs alone, and what the buyer gets is only that fractional, undivided interest, not a right to immediately walk in and occupy any specific part of the house or land. Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 says exactly this, and it is the starting point for every dispute of this kind.

The remedies available to the other co-owners depend heavily on what kind of property is involved and what the buyer tries to do next. A buyer who tries to move into joint possession of a family dwelling house faces a different, and more restricted, legal position than a buyer of an undivided share in open land or a commercial building. This guide works through both situations, and the separate route of a partition suit that is always available regardless of how the sale happened.

sections.heading: What a co-owner's sale actually transfers
paragraphs: Under Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, a co-owner who transfers their share acquires for the transferee only the transferring co-owner's own right in the property, along with that co-owner's existing right to joint possession or other common or part-enjoyment of the property, and subject to the conditions and liabilities attaching to that share. In plain terms, the buyer steps into the shoes of the selling co-owner, no more and no less. If the seller owned one-third of a plot, the buyer gets a one-third undivided interest, not a marked-off one-third of the land, and not the right to deal with the other two-thirds.

This means a sale by one co-owner, by itself, does not extinguish or dilute the other co-owners' shares, and it does not need their signature or consent to be valid as between the seller and the buyer. What it does create, in many cases, is a new and sometimes unwelcome co-owner in place of the old one, which is exactly what drives families and business partners to court when they find out after the fact.

sections.heading: The dwelling house exception: the second limb of Section 44
paragraphs: Section 44 carries a second paragraph aimed specifically at family dwelling houses. Where the property is a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family and a co-owner transfers their share to someone who is a stranger to that family, the second paragraph provides that the transferee does not get the right to joint possession or common enjoyment of the house, even though they have validly bought the share. The remaining family members can keep the stranger-buyer out of physical occupation of the house, even while that buyer legitimately owns an undivided interest in it on paper.

The Supreme Court applied exactly this principle in Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden (1990), holding that where the property in question is a dwelling house of an undivided family and the transfer is to a stranger, a court can grant a mandatory interlocutory injunction restraining that stranger transferee from entering into or remaining in possession of the house. The Court treated this as an exceptional remedy, available on a stronger showing than an ordinary prohibitory injunction, but available nonetheless specifically because of what the second paragraph of Section 44 protects.

This exception only helps where the property genuinely is a dwelling house of an undivided family and the buyer genuinely is a stranger to that family. It does not apply to open agricultural land, a commercial building, or a dwelling house that has already been partitioned by metes and bounds between the co-owners, since in that situation each owner holds a defined, separate portion rather than an undivided share in a common family home.

sections.heading: Buying out the stranger: the Partition Act route
paragraphs: Where a stranger has bought a share in a dwelling house of an undivided family and then sues for partition of their share, Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 gives the other members of the family an option: they can apply to the court to have the stranger's share valued and bought out, so that the house stays within the family rather than being physically divided with an outsider holding a slice of it. This remedy operates specifically at the stage when the stranger transferee moves for partition, and the Supreme Court has discussed its scope and limits in Gautam Paul v. Debi Rani Paul, which practitioners read as confining Section 4 to that partition-suit stage rather than letting a family pre-emptively force a buyout the moment they learn of the sale.

In practice, this means a family that wants to keep an outsider from ever getting a foothold in the house has two separate tools working at different points: an injunction under the second paragraph of Section 44 to keep the stranger out of physical possession from the start, and the Section 4 buyout option if and when that stranger goes to court seeking partition.

sections.heading: Outside the dwelling house exception: when the sale simply stands
paragraphs: For property that is not a family dwelling house, the position is less protective of the other co-owners. A co-owner's sale of their own undivided share in agricultural land, a commercial plot, or a building that is not a residence occupied by the family, is generally effective, and the buyer steps into co-ownership alongside the remaining owners, with the same right to joint possession and common enjoyment the seller had. The remaining co-owners cannot undo that sale merely because they were not consulted or would have preferred to buy the share themselves, since Indian law, outside specific statutory pre-emption schemes that apply in particular states or particular categories of agricultural land, does not generally give co-owners a right of first refusal over each other's shares.

What the remaining co-owners can realistically do in this situation is seek a partition, forcing a division of the whole property, by metes and bounds where that is practicable or by sale with division of proceeds where it is not, so that everyone's share becomes a defined, separate holding rather than an ongoing undivided interest shared with someone they did not choose as a co-owner.

sections.heading: Partition as the general remedy, and what to do before a sale happens
paragraphs: A partition suit is open to any co-owner at any time, filed before or after a problematic sale, and it remains the most reliable way to end an unwanted co-ownership regardless of how it arose. Our separate guide on how partition suits work in India covers who can file, how the court decides between dividing the property physically and ordering its sale, and how the process runs from filing to final decree, and that process applies here just as it would to any other co-ownership dispute.

If you learn that a co-owner is about to sell, rather than having already sold, your practical options are narrower but real: you can approach the court for an injunction restraining the specific co-owner from completing an unauthorised transfer where the facts support it, or you can move quickly to put the intending buyer on notice of the family's position, particularly where the property is a dwelling house, so that any buyer proceeds, if at all, with clear knowledge of exactly what interest they are and are not acquiring.

faqs.q: Can my brother sell his share in our family house without asking me?
faqs.a: Yes, he can sell his own undivided share without your consent, and that sale is valid to that extent. But if the house is a dwelling house of an undivided family and the buyer is a stranger to the family, you can seek an injunction to keep that buyer out of physical possession, even though the sale of the share itself stands.

faqs.q: Does a co-owner need the other co-owners' signatures to sell their share?
faqs.a: No. A co-owner's own undivided share can be sold without the other co-owners joining the sale deed or consenting to it. Their signatures are needed only if the sale is meant to transfer the whole property, not just that one co-owner's share.

faqs.q: What can I do if a stranger has already bought my brother's share in our family home?
faqs.a: If the property is a dwelling house of an undivided family, you can seek an injunction against the stranger-buyer taking joint possession, as the Supreme Court allowed in Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden. If that buyer later sues for partition, the Partition Act also lets the family apply to buy out the stranger's share instead of dividing the house.

faqs.q: Is there a right of first refusal for co-owners in India before a sale to an outsider?
faqs.a: Generally no, outside specific state laws or categories such as some agricultural tenancy statutes. A co-owner can usually sell their undivided share to anyone without first offering it to the other co-owners, except where a particular state law creates a pre-emption right for the type of property involved.

Partition Act, 1893, Section 4, on the right of family members to buy out a stranger transferee's share before partition

verification_notes: The core rule that a co-owner's sale transfers only their own undivided share and the rights attaching to it, under Section 44: confirmed from the statute's text as summarised consistently across casemine.com and thelegallock.com, both describing the same scope.

The second paragraph's dwelling house exception, restricting a stranger transferee's right to joint possession: confirmed from two independent sources (casemine.com and mahendrabhavsar.com) describing the same restriction in materially identical terms.

Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden (AIR 1990 SC 867) and its holding on mandatory interlocutory injunctions against a stranger transferee of a dwelling house share: confirmed from two independent secondary sources (lexibal.com and a lawtext.in-reported summary) describing the same case name, the same statutory basis, and the same remedy; the full judgment text was not independently opened, so the precise reasoning beyond this summary should be checked against the reported judgment before being relied on in a specific matter.

Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 and its operation at the stage when a stranger transferee sues for partition, with Gautam Paul v. Debi Rani Paul cited as discussing its scope: confirmed from a single secondary commentary describing this case and holding; a second independent source naming the same case was not found in the search results, so this citation rests on one reported source and should be verified against the judgment before being cited as settled authority in any filing.

The absence of a general co-owner right of first refusal under Indian law outside specific state or category-based pre-emption schemes: this is stated as a general proposition consistent with the sources reviewed, which did not surface any contrary general pre-emption rule, though state-specific tenancy or agricultural land statutes can and do create such rights in particular contexts, which this guide notes rather than overstates.

Partition as the general remedy regardless of how the co-ownership dispute arose: this is standard, well-settled procedural law rather than a point needing case-specific verification, and is treated accordingly.
